Other information

Change to make CSS url() functions accept optional request modifiers after the quoted URL string: cross-origin(), integrity(), and referrer-policy(). These modifiers control the fetch behavior of the referenced resource directly from CSS, without requiring changes to HTML markup or JavaScript. For example, background-image: url("image.png" cross-origin(anonymous)) fetches the image using CORS anonymous mode.

Specification title

fetch

Specification or proposal URL (if available)

whatwg/fetch#1854

Explainer URL (if available)

No response

Proposal author(s)

@pmeenan

MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Compression_dictionary_transport

Caniuse.com URL

No response

Bugzilla URL

No response

Mozillians who can provide input

No response

WebKit standards-position

WebKit/standards-positions#644

Other information

This is a change to Compression Dictionary Transport that we talked about during the fetch spec integration for the browser-specific CORS readability issues that are not covered by the RFC.

Current WPT's and Chrome's implementation do not allow dictionary compression for cross-origin no-cors requests to prevent oracle attacks (and clients don't send the Accept-Encoding or dictionary headers for those requests).

At TPAC 2025 in the TAG general discussion, we came up with a solution of leveraging the existing Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin response header to flag responses that don't need protection from oracle attacks (the current use for this header) since they contain only public data.

The current PR for the Compression Dictionary Transport spec integration into fetch includes the change but it was not part of the original WPT's or implementations so I wanted to get buy-in on the change (and provide notice for the in-flight implementation work).

If we ever want to enable dictionary compression for some no-cors requests, now is the time to do it before there are widespread deployments.

The only risk is if there are resources that are used in both same-origin and cross-origin no-cors contexts and the origin currently supports compression dictionary transport but does not have the CORP response header on the responses, it will start to fail if they are not limiting dictionary support to same-origin responses (required by the RFC but unlikely someone would notice since they don't get the headers currently if it's not supported).

Going forward it wouldn't be a problem because the issue would be discovered at the time of deployment rather that with a browser change to existing production traffic.

There aren't any deployments that I'm aware of that have that problem but the risk of it happening increases over time with more dictionary deployments, limiting the chances of making the change in the future.

The alternative would be to not allow dictionary compression for any cross-origin no-cors requests independent of the content which would be cleaner for sites since they'd never get the dictionary request headers but it also limits the ability for third-party script embeds to use dictionary compression.
items.title: Compression Dictionary support for cross-origin no-cors requests

Platform-provided behaviors for custom elements

Specification or proposal URL (if available)

whatwg/html#12150

Explainer URL (if available)

No response

Mozillians who can provide input

WebKit standards-position

WebKit/standards-positions#642

Other information

Custom element authors frequently need their elements to leverage platform behaviors that are currently exclusive to native HTML elements, such as form submission, popover invocation, label behaviors, form semantics, and radio button grouping. This proposal introduces platform-provided behaviors as a mechanism for autonomous custom elements to adopt specific native HTML element behaviors. Rather than requiring developers to reimplement native behaviors in JavaScript or extend native elements (customized built-ins), this approach exposes native capabilities as composable behaviors.

Specification title

Web Application Manifest

Specification or proposal URL (if available)

https://pr-preview.s3.amazonaws.com/w3c/manifest/pull/1206.html#installation-events

Explainer URL (if available)

No response

Proposal author(s)

@christianliebel (I’m not the author of BIP, but a co-editor of the Manifest spec)

MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/BeforeInstallPromptEvent

Caniuse.com URL

https://caniuse.com/mdn-api_beforeinstallpromptevent_prompt

Bugzilla URL

https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1967146

Mozillians who can provide input

@saschanaz @drubino-mozilla

WebKit standards-position

WebKit/standards-positions#619

Other information

The WebApps Working Group is currently discussing ways to programmatically trigger an install prompt. During a recent call, the meeting participants favored exploring using the existing BeforeInstallPromptEvent (BIP) for the “installing the current app” use case due to its existing usage. Vendors were asked to clarify their positions on BIP.

The name beforeinstallprompt is historical and refers to prompts that user agents previously showed. The event is now fired deterministically in Chromium (when certain promotability criteria are met). After the event is fired, the developer can call the prompt() method on the event interface to show the user agent’s install prompt.

Screen recording of the BIP flow

In this screen recording, the beforeinstallprompt event has already been fired. After receiving the event, the authors show an “install” button. When the user clicks this button, the prompt() method is called on the event interface, and the user agent’s install prompt is shown.

macOS.Chromium.beforeinstallprompt.mov

BIP usage data

BIP has been available in Chromium-based browsers since 2015. HTTP Archive data shows that BIP is used on 5.12% of all desktop and 4.78% of all mobile sites in the HTTP Archive dataset (July 2025 crawl, source). If BIP were standardized, the existing install promotion of these sites would “just work” in other browsers.

TAG review

There is no specific review of beforeinstallprompt, but reviews of other proposals covering the same underlying same-origin install use case previously concluded with “satisfied”.

Alternative APIs

  • navigator.install() – imperative API
  • <install> – declarative API
items.title: Web Application Manifest - `BeforeInstallPromptEvent`
